story:
This tree cost forty cents. The University of Wisconsin Arboretum bought it as a seedling in 1956, grew it on in the nursery for five years, and on 3 October 1961 moved it to the corner of the ground where the Visitor Center now stands. It has not moved since.

Black tupelo barely belongs in Wisconsin. In the wild it grows in a single county, Kenosha, in the state's south-east corner. This planted one has done well enough to become the champion of its species in the Wisconsin DNR register, at 1.61 metres round, 11.9 metres tall, with a crown about 13.5 metres across. It is one of two state champions in the Arboretum's Longenecker Horticultural Gardens.

The Arboretum later named the selection 'Carolyn', after a granddaughter of a former curator, though its own accounts differ on which granddaughter. A male tupelo was planted nearby to give it pollen. Stock grown from the tree went to the nursery trade, with royalties paid back to the Arboretum, so the forty-cent seedling has more than earned its price.

The register's curator noted it alive and well in February 2021, and a visitor photographed it in October 2026. Its age comes from paperwork rather than an estimate. Bought in 1956, it is about seventy, plus however old it was when it arrived.
name: The Carolyn Black Tupelo

story:
This ash is alive because somebody keeps it that way. It is one of three ash trees in the Longenecker Horticultural Gardens that the University of Wisconsin Arboretum treats against emerald ash borer, the beetle that kills ash, and it is the biggest blue ash the Wisconsin DNR champion register knows.

Its paperwork is unusually complete. It grew from seed of a blue ash at the Morton Arboretum outside Chicago. The US Department of Agriculture sent the young tree to Madison in 1960, and it went into the ground in the Gardens on 4 November 1968. That makes it somewhere around sixty, older by however long it waited as nursery stock.

Blue ash is a rarity this far north. Wisconsin has it wild in one county only, Waukesha. The register measured this one at 1.79 metres round and 13.4 metres tall, with a crown about 15 metres across, and with the black tupelo by the Visitor Center it is one of the Gardens' two state champions.

The tell is in the twigs, which are four-sided, square in section, as blue ash twigs are. We have not pinned down which trunk in the collection is the champion, so the square twigs are the surest guide. A visitor recorded it in September 2024.
name: The Blue Ash of Longenecker Gardens

story:
Wisconsin's champion pin oak grows in a small memorial park on the University of Wisconsin campus, and its crown is wider than the tree is tall. The state's DNR champion register measured a trunk 3.94 metres round, a height of 25.4 metres, and a crown about 30 metres one way and 26 the other.

It is one of three oaks standing together in the centre of Camp Randall Memorial Park, the one to the south-west. The register's point falls beside the park's Civil War cannon on North Randall Avenue, so this is the park and not the stadium of the same name. The other two oaks have never been measured, and nobody can say how close they come.

For scale, the champion pin oak of the Forest Preserves of Cook County, on our Chicago page, is 3.59 metres round. This one is about a third of a metre thicker, on a shorter tree.

The register is the only written record of it, and it does not say when the tape went round. A visitor photographed an oak at this spot in June 2026. In October the leaves turn dark red to russet, which is the best time to come. Nobody has published an age. If you know when these three oaks were planted, or whether they were here before the park, tell us.

story:
Ponderosa pine is a tree of the American West, and Wisconsin's champion of the species grows behind a garden building on the University of Wisconsin campus in Madison. Somebody planted it here, far from its native range. The Wisconsin DNR champion register measured it at 2.50 metres round and 19.1 metres tall, with a narrow crown about 11 metres across.

It stands at the north-west corner of Allen Centennial Garden and carries the university plant tag 56-1527. That number is tempting. A 56 at the front looks like the year 1956, and it may well be, but nothing we have read says so, which is why we give this pine no age. A tag is a filing number until somebody shows it is a date.

Allen Centennial Garden is the university's public garden, free and open from dawn to dusk every day, so the pine is easy to visit. The register describes it as behind the building; look on the garden side.

The register is the only record of the tree and does not say when it was measured. A visitor photographed it in October 2026. If you know when it went in, or what that tag really means, tell us.

story:
When the City of Madison handed out its first Heritage Tree Awards in 2012, the prize for history went to a hackberry on a grass strip beside the street. It is also the biggest of its species in the Wisconsin DNR champion register, at 3.85 metres round and 30.2 metres tall, with a crown about 20 metres across.

The history comes from the family who nominated it. By their account the tree was planted more than a hundred years ago by the man who had the first house built in the Oakland development, in 1897. That is a family memory rather than a record, so treat 1897 as a ceiling rather than a date. If they are right, the hackberry is somewhere between about a hundred and 129 years old, and it has seen the whole neighbourhood go up around it.

It stands on the city's terrace on the Madison Street side of the corner with Oakland Avenue, in front of a private house. Look from the sidewalk; the yard behind it is somebody's home. The bark rewards a close look even from there, corky and warty, the hackberry's signature.

A visitor recorded it in April 2025. The register does not say when it was measured.

Nominatim places the pin beside a Madison St house, so pin is approximate on the corner. iNaturalist 2025-04-12 near pin (alive).
